newsitem.title: HONG KONG: INTERVIEW - Asian bond issuers woo US investors.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Asian bond issuers woo US investors.

text.p: Asian bond issuers, both the new and the more experienced, are wooing U.S. investors as a way to raise long-term money and diversify their investor base, said Mark Schneider, vice president at J.P. Morgan Securities.

"If you look at some of the frequent borrowers, the investor diversification is particularly compelling. They may be looking at massive capital expenditure programmes over a number of years so they want to be sure the investor base is there when they need it," said Schneider, who is based in New York.
But even less frequent borrowers that typically rely on Asian investors can find value in diversification, he said.
The U.S. market also offers extremely long maturities. A few Asian issuers, notably China and Malaysia's Tenaga Nasional, already have issued 100-year bonds in the U.S.
"There are a number of very long dated deals that are getting done that quite frankly could not have been done a few years ago," said Schneider.
"And that is the ultimate attraction of the U.S., that there is no competition for long-dated paper," he said.
For the Asian borrower, U.S. investors' receptiveness to structured transactions that may, for example, include put and other options, also is a distinct advantage, Schneider said.

Some 65 investors, mostly from the U.S., are travelling to six Asian cities this week to hear Asian sovereigns, banks and corporations make their case as part of an investor "roadshow" sponsored by J.P. Morgan.

Issuers making presentations in Hong Kong include the Ministry of Finance of China, Malaysia's Tenaga, Hong Kong's China Light and Power and Mass Transit Railway Corp and South Korea quasi-sovereigns Korea Development Bank and Korea Electric Power Co.

All of these issuers have tapped the Yankee market in the past, but many of the borrowers making presentations later this week in Manila, Jakarta, Bangkok, New Delhi and Bombay would be debut issuers in the U.S. public or private placement markets.

Examples include the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand (EGAT), the Indonesian state banks, Indian policy banks such as ICICI and IDBI and Indian energy companies Oil and Natural Gas Corp and Indian Oil Corp, Schneider said.
For new investors unfamiliar with Asia, the most common questions concern the credit quality of the sovereign.

"It doesn't matter if it is BB-India or AA-Korea, it's going to be the same question. For the new investor, about 70 percent of the focus is on the sovereign risk and 30 percent on the corporate risk," he said.
India is rated Baa3 by Moody's Investors Service and BB-plus by Standard and Poor's Corp, while South Korea is assessed at A1 and AA-minus by the rating agencies, respectively.
For the more experienced investor, the focus is the other way around, with more attention paid to corporate risk.
Up to now, most issuers in the U.S. Yankee market have been investment grade, but lesser-rated borrowers can, and have, successfully tapped the market.
"The number of below-investment grade companies accessing the U.S. market is a much bigger percentage than it was five years ago when it was probably close to zero," said Schneider.
"Will that percentage ever become half? I would say no. But the U.S. is the only game in town for the long-dated sub-investment grade market," he added.
Schneider speculated that of the issuers participating in the roadshow, most will try to place bonds in the U.S. in 1997 while a few may be thinking more in terms of 1998.

"Some of these people are going to do deals in the first half next year. Others will be just testing the waters as a way to get to know the investors," he said. "For these, it is still the early days."
-- Hong Kong Newsroom (852) 2843-6371
